claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous, fine-grained fcc microstructure.
The as-built alloy possesses a thin native oxide layer.
Degradation during elevated-temperature gas exposure is governed by oxygen transport along grain boundaries.
In oxidizing atmospheres, rapid grain-boundary oxidation forms continuous brittle oxide films.
The intergranular oxide films may consist of Cr2O3 and/or TiO2.
Continuous grain-boundary oxide films weaken intergranular cohesion.
Weakened intergranular cohesion promotes early crack initiation and oxide spallation.
In reducing environments, the alloy lacks an effective protective oxide film.
The absence of a protective film in reducing environments permits deeper oxygen penetration and internal oxidation.
Internal oxidation in reducing environments forms discrete oxide precipitates.
Internal oxide precipitates destabilize the fcc matrix.
Both the oxidizing-atmosphere and reducing-atmosphere pathways can lead to catastrophic failure.
Higher oxygen partial pressure will produce thicker and more continuous intergranular oxide films than the starting-state baseline.
Exposure at higher oxygen partial pressure will reduce fracture toughness relative to the starting-state baseline.
Reducing-atmosphere exposure will produce more dispersed internal oxide precipitates than the starting-state baseline.
Reducing-atmosphere exposure will cause mechanical degradation similar to that caused by oxidizing-atmosphere exposure.
Oxide morphology will correlate with reductions in structural and mechanical performance before catastrophic failure.
The proposed behavior applies at approximately 700–900 °C for exposures lasting several hours.
Outside the stated temperature or duration regime, alternative degradation mechanisms may dominate.
Additive-manufacturing-derived microstructural variation, elemental segregation, and residual stress may alter oxidation behavior.

contradictions.description: The prediction says oxidizing and reducing exposures may cause similar mechanical degradation, while the falsification rule requires a corresponding differential degradation in mechanical properties. Similar degradation could therefore both satisfy the prediction and trigger falsification.
